To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binding of La3+, a trivalent lanthanide cation, to the erythrocyte membrane induces a Ca2+ binding process to the cytoskeletal protein, which results in a significant increase in the incorporation of 1C-glucose and 14C-glutamate into the cytoskeleton.
the La3+-induced Ca2 binding to the cyto-skeleton of erythrocytes, in contrast to the known Ca2+-dependent binding, is independent of ATP and does not involve the Ca2+ channel.
the Ca2+ binding sites in the red blood cells are located in the cytoskeleton, and that the Ca2+-dependent binding sites are located in the outer surface of the cell membrane.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of La3+ in the Ca2+ binding and metabolism of the erythrocyte skeleton.
the study of the effect of La3+ ions on Ca2+ binding and the incorporation of 45Ca2+ into the cytoskeletons of human and rat red blood cells.
the role of La3+ in the regulation of calcium homeostasis in human red cells and the possible role of the metal in the mechanism of Ca2+ transport in the cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the binding of La3+, a non-permeant cation, to the outer surface membrane of erythrocytes results in a Ca2+ binding, a process which is mediated by ATP and is associated with the formation of Ca2+-ATP complexes.
the La3+ binding to the outer surface membrane of erythrocytes leads to an activation of the Ca2+ binding sites of cytoskeleton proteins.
Ca2+ binding in the cytoskeleton is not the only factor responsible for the observed changes in the erythrocyte skeleton.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
La3+ is a new type of calcium ionophore.
La3+ is able to induce Ca2+ binding and Ca2+ binding is able to enhance the glycolytic activity.
the Ca2+-binding protein(s) of the red blood cell cytoskeleton is/are sensitive to the La3+ ion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ binding in the presence of La3+ is a novel process, which may have a significant role in the regulation of Ca2+ transport and/or Ca2+ binding sites.

La(3+), which is a well-known Ca(2+) antagonist, is able to bind to the erythrocyte skeleton, thus suggesting that Ca(2+) binding sites in the erythrocytes may not be identical with those in other cells.
La3+ is a potent activator of the Ca2+ binding and the incorporation of 45Ca2+ into the erythrocyte skeleton.
